Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The patient shows a partial radiologic response of liver metastases after intensive chemotherapy (three lesions disappeared, the remaining lesions reduced by ~40 % and are now hypo‑intense). This suggests that a curative‑intent liver operation could become feasible, but decisive anatomic and functional information is lacking. Specifically, the analysis does not provide (a) the exact hepatic segments involved, the size of each remaining lesion, or any vascular/biliary contact; (b) a volumetric assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR ratio); (c) the status of the rectal primary (resected or not) and its molecular profile; and (d) a complete extra‑hepatic staging (chest CT, abdomen CT, peritoneal, nodal, bone, brain). Because these missing data directly determine whether an adequate oncologic and functional resection can be performed, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the required assessments.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging work‑up  
   • Perform a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, nodal, peritoneal, bone or brain metastases.  
   • Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and volumetric analysis to define the exact number, size, segmental distribution of residual lesions, vascular/biliary involvement, and calculate the FLR ratio.  
   • Assess the rectal primary: if not yet resected, schedule pelvic MRI/endorectal ultrasound and consider neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy according to rectal cancer guidelines.  
   • Obtain molecular profiling (RAS, BRAF, MSI) and tumor grade from biopsy or prior pathology to guide systemic therapy and potential targeted agents.  

2. Systemic therapy continuation (conversion intent)  
   • Continue the current FOLFOXIRI regimen for 2–3 additional cycles, monitoring CEA trend and imaging response.  
   • If molecular testing reveals RAS wild‑type, consider adding anti‑EGFR therapy; if MSI‑high, evaluate eligibility for immunotherapy.  

3. Re‑assessment after additional systemic cycles  
   • Repeat liver MRI with volumetry and chest‑abdomen CT.  
   • If the FLR is ≥30 % (≥40 % in patients with chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) and no extra‑hepatic disease is identified, proceed to curative surgery.  

4. Surgical plan (conditional on re‑assessment)  
   • Primary rectal tumor: perform total mesorectal excision (TME) either before, simultaneously, or after liver resection depending on tumor location, response, and patient fitness.  
   • Liver metastases: aim for parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy targeting all radiologically visible lesions; consider intra‑operative ultrasound to detect disappearing lesions and treat them with ablation if necessary.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) before definitive resection.  

5. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy  
   • Resume systemic therapy (or switch to maintenance) after recovery, guided by pathology (margin status, response grade) and molecular profile.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Precise hepatic segmental involvement, lesion sizes, and presence of vascular or biliary invasion (needed to determine technical resectability).  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volumetric ratio (determines functional safety of hepatectomy).  
- Status of the rectal primary tumor (resected vs. pending) and need for neoadjuvant pelvic therapy.  
- Comprehensive extra‑hepatic staging (chest/abdomen CT, PET‑CT) to exclude distant disease.  
- Molecular phenotype and tumor grade (inform systemic regimen and targeted options).  
These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI.
B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
E. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor.
F. a chest CT scan
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation
I. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
J. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: Both recommendations classify the case as potentially resectable and propose similar management sequences. Completeness: Both cover resectability assessment, preoperative staging (liver MRI, chest CT, FLR), surgical strategy (parenchymal-sparing, staged hepatectomy, intraoperative ultrasound), systemic therapy continuation, and post-operative considerations. Step concordance: Both agree on 'potentially resectable' status and propose the same sequence: expert restaging first, then surgical planning conditional on FLR and complete clearance feasibility, with continuation of systemic therapy if not resectable. Case tailoring: Both address disappearing lesions requiring localization, bilobar disease considerations, molecular profiling (RAS, MSI), rectal primary status, and parenchymal-sparing approach. Missing data concordance: Both identify the same core missing elements: exact segmental distribution of lesions, FLR volumetry, vascular/biliary relationships, rectal primary status, chest CT/extrahepatic staging, and molecular profile. Recommendation 2 adds some additional items (ctDNA, liquid biopsy, CEA evolution) but these are supplementary rather than contradictory, and the core missing data overlap is substantial enough to consider them aligned.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient now has three liver lesions <2 cm after a major response to chemotherapy, which in principle could be amenable to curative‑intent liver resection. However, decisive information required for a definitive surgical plan is missing: (a) complete thoraco‑abdominal staging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) to exclude extra‑hepatic disease; (b) detailed hepatic anatomy (segments involved, vascular or biliary contact, arterial anatomy) and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant; (c) status of the rectal primary (resected or still in situ, presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms). Because these items are essential to determine whether an R0 liver resection can be performed safely, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending acquisition of the missing data.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Continue systemic therapy (e.g., 2–4 additional cycles of the current regimen) to consolidate the radiologic and CEA response, unless toxicity or patient preference dictates otherwise.  
• At the end of the consolidation phase obtain a full staging work‑up:  
   – Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or bone metastases.  
   – High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and 3‑D volumetry to define exact segmental location of each lesion, relationship to portal/hepatic veins, biliary structures, and to calculate FLR ratio.  
   – Endoscopic evaluation of the rectal primary (rigid sigmoidoscopy or MRI pelvis) to determine if the primary tumor has been resected, its T/N stage, and whether neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy is indicated.  
• Multidisciplinary decision based on restaging:  
   – If extra‑hepatic disease is absent and FLR ≥30 % (or ≥20 % in a normal liver) with no major vascular/biliary involvement, proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery. Plan a parenchymal‑sparing approach (segmental or non‑anatomic wedge resections) to achieve R0 margins while preserving liver function; intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to confirm lesion location and guide resection.  
   – If the rectal primary remains unresected or symptomatic, schedule neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by total mesorectal excision (TME) either before or after liver resection, depending on timing and patient fitness.  
   – If extra‑hepatic metastases are identified, shift to systemic therapy with possible targeted agents (RAS wild‑type) and consider metastasectomy only for isolated, resectable lesions after systemic control.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Status of the rectal primary tumor (resected vs. still present, symptom burden, need for neoadjuvant radiotherapy).  
• Complete thoraco‑abdominal imaging to confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Detailed hepatic segmental involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and arterial anatomy.  
• Quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric data.  
• Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (prognostic relevance).  

These missing items are pivotal to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: Completeness: Both recommendations cover the major clinical domains including resectability assessment, preoperative staging (imaging), surgical management, systemic therapy, and management of the rectal primary. Recommendation 2 adds postoperative pathology considerations, prehabilitation/ERAS, minimally invasive approaches, and liquid biopsy, but the core domains are substantially covered in both. Step concordance: The two recommendations diverge on the resectability assessment in Step 1. Recommendation 1 classifies the patient as 'potentially resectable' pending missing data, while Recommendation 2 classifies the patient as 'resectable' (pending volumetric reassessment). This is a meaningful clinical distinction. Additionally, Recommendation 2 emphasizes treating all original metastatic sites including disappeared metastases, which is not highlighted in Recommendation 1, and proposes a staged hepatectomy consideration absent from Recommendation 1. Recommendation 1 proposes continuing systemic therapy for consolidation before restaging, while Recommendation 2 proceeds directly to restaging and surgery. These differences in clinical reasoning steps and sequence represent a lack of step-by-step concordance. Case-tailoring concordance: Both recommendations address case-specific elements such as molecular profile implications (RAS/MSI status), lesion-specific surgical considerations (parenchymal-sparing, intraoperative ultrasound), management of the rectal primary, and CEA response. Both are well-tailored to the specific clinical scenario. Missing data concordance: Both recommendations identify the same essential missing information: segmental distribution and vascular/biliary relationships of lesions, FLR estimation, status/treatment of the rectal primary, extrahepatic disease assessment via chest CT, and tumor differentiation/molecular profile. Recommendation 2 adds liquid biopsy and specific rectal parameters (CRM, distance from anal verge), but the core missing data items are substantially aligned.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The liver shows a single progressing lesion (segment VII, 5 cm) after systemic therapy, while the other lesions have either disappeared or are stable, suggesting that a curative‑intent liver operation could be feasible. However, decisive information required to confirm surgical feasibility is missing: (a) thoraco‑abdominal staging (thoracic CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases, (b) future liver remnant (FLR) volume assessment, (c) detailed vascular anatomy and possible portal/hepatic vein involvement of the segment VII lesion, (d) status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or still in situ). Because these items must be clarified or addressed before a definitive operation, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Complete staging: obtain a thoracic CT scan (or PET‑CT) and a liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to evaluate extra‑hepatic disease, lesion vascular contact, and precise hepatic anatomy.  
• Assess FLR: perform volumetric CT or MRI; if FLR is <30 % in a normal liver, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) as needed.  
• Primary tumor management: if the left‑sided primary has not yet been resected, schedule a left hemicolectomy. Timing can be simultaneous with liver resection if the patient’s condition permits and the liver surgery is limited; otherwise, perform the colorectal resection first, followed by liver surgery after recovery.  
• Systemic therapy: continue or intensify conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) while awaiting restaging, aiming to maintain disease control of the six stable lesions and to attempt further downsizing of the progressing segment VII lesion. Monitor CEA trends.  
• Liver‑directed treatment:  
   – If FLR is adequate and vascular involvement is absent, proceed with a parenchymal‑sparing anatomical resection of the segment VII lesion (segmentectomy or extended segmentectomy) together with resection of any residual visible metastases.  
   – If FLR is insufficient or the lesion abuts major vessels, consider local ablative therapy (microwave or radiofrequency ablation) for the 5 cm lesion, possibly combined with limited resection of other residual lesions.  
• Post‑operative plan: after liver surgery (or ablation) and primary resection, resume adjuvant systemic chemotherapy for at least 6 months, adjusting regimen based on response and molecular profile (KRAS‑mutated).  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
• Liver MRI with vascular phase to define vascular contact/invasion of the segment VII lesion.  
• Quantitative FLR ratio to confirm that the remaining liver volume will be sufficient after resection.  
• Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs. still present) and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms.  
• Histologic grade of differentiation and baseline CEA level for prognostic and monitoring purposes.  
These missing items are the most critical to finalize resectability and to tailor the operative and systemic treatment plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: Completeness: Both recommendations cover the major clinical domains including resectability assessment, staging/imaging, systemic therapy, surgical/local management, and missing data. While Recommendation 2 lacks explicit mention of postoperative adjuvant therapy, both cover the main management components sufficiently to be considered substantially complete. Step-by-step concordance: The two recommendations diverge at Step 1 - Recommendation 1 classifies the case as 'potentially resectable' with curative intent possible, while Recommendation 2 classifies it as 'unresectable at this stage' due to multifocal disease and inadequate FLR concerns. This fundamental difference in resectability assessment leads to different management sequences in Step 2, with Recommendation 1 proposing a more aggressive curative-intent approach and Recommendation 2 proposing cytoreduction or systemic control first. This is a significant discordance in clinical reasoning. Case-tailoring concordance: Both recommendations address case-specific elements including the segment VII progressing lesion, molecular profile (KRAS), FLR assessment, primary tumor status, and treatment sequencing considerations. Both are appropriately tailored to the clinical scenario. Missing data concordance: Both recommendations identify similar critical missing information including thoracic/extrahepatic staging, FLR estimation, status of primary tumor, vascular anatomy of segment VII lesion, and molecular/histologic profile. Recommendation 2 additionally mentions performance status and liquid biopsy, but the core missing data points are concordant.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The current data show a radiologic complete response of bilobar liver metastases after FOLFOXIRI, but critical information required to determine surgical feasibility is missing. Specifically, the status of the rectal primary (whether it has already been resected), the detailed hepatic lesion characteristics (number, size, vascular contact, FLR ratio), and a dedicated liver MRI are absent. Because these pieces of information are decisive for planning either simultaneous or staged resection, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront” and does not meet criteria for “Not resectable.”  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences (and, if available, gadoxetate‑enhanced imaging) to confirm true pathological complete response and to assess FLR volume.  
- Perform a pelvic MRI and endoscopic evaluation of the rectal lesion to define T/N stage, circumferential resection margin risk, and to decide whether the primary tumor has already been removed.  
- If the rectal primary has not been resected and is locally advanced, deliver long‑course chemoradiotherapy (capecitabine‑based) followed by total mesorectal excision (TME).  
- Based on the liver MRI:  
   • If no residual disease is identified and FLR is adequate, adopt a watch‑and‑wait strategy for the liver with serial imaging (CT/MRI every 3 months) and continue systemic therapy as per standard adjuvant protocols.  
   • If residual lesions are detected, plan a parenchymal‑sparing liver resection (or two‑stage/ALPPS if FLR insufficient) after confirming adequate FLR ratio; intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to detect occult disease.  
- Continue systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 2–3 additional cycles of FOLFOXIRI or switch to a maintenance regimen) while awaiting definitive imaging and primary‑tumor work‑up, especially if high‑risk molecular features are later identified.  
- Consider adjuvant therapy guided by final pathology (e.g., oxaliplatin‑based regimen, targeted agents if KRAS/NRAS/BRAF status warrants).  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Status of the rectal primary tumor resection (has it been removed?).  
- Molecular phenotype of the primary (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status) and grade of differentiation.  
- Dedicated liver MRI findings (number, size, vascular involvement, presence of fibrosis/necrosis).  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and ratio compatibility with surgery.  
- Detailed hepatic lesion count and dimensions to confirm true complete response.  
- Brain imaging results (to rule out occult cerebral metastasis).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bilobar liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, CT shows complete radiological disappearance of all lesions and CEA has normalized. Despite this apparent complete response, the high risk of occult residual microscopic disease at the sites of the initial metastases makes the situation potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely classifiable as disease-free without precise remapping of the original disease.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences and compare meticulously with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, even if no lesion is currently visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial lesions on baseline imaging.
B. Precise localization of the initial metastases relative to vascular structures.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor : circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
E. Patient’s performance status for potential staged hepatectomy.
F. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: Completeness: Both recommendations cover the major clinical domains including resectability assessment, preoperative staging (liver MRI, pelvic MRI), surgical management (parenchymal-sparing, intraoperative ultrasound, staged approach), rectal primary management, and postoperative therapy. They are substantially complete and cover the same major components. Step concordance: Both classify the case as 'potentially resectable' after conversion therapy, both recommend liver MRI with DWI as mandatory restaging, both address parenchymal-sparing hepatectomy with intraoperative ultrasound, both integrate rectal primary management, and both discuss postoperative systemic therapy. The clinical reasoning sequence is aligned. Case-tailoring: Recommendation 2 includes additional case-specific details absent from Recommendation 1, such as: PRODIGE 23 protocol reference, specific rectal response categories (complete/near-complete/incomplete morphological response) with tailored management for each, minimally invasive approach for rectal resection, prehabilitation and ERAS protocols, histological growth pattern and TRG scoring in pathology, and liquid biopsy/ctDNA considerations. Recommendation 1 discusses brain imaging and molecular phenotype implications more explicitly. These differences reflect meaningful divergence in case-specific tailoring. Missing data concordance: Both identify liver MRI findings, FLR estimation, rectal primary status, and extrahepatic disease as missing. However, Recommendation 2 uniquely identifies patient performance status, liquid biopsy/ctDNA, and precise segmental/vascular localization of initial lesions, while Recommendation 1 uniquely identifies brain imaging, molecular profile (KRAS/NRAS/BRAF/MSI), and tumor grade/differentiation. These differences are substantive enough to consider them discordant in missing data identification.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, history of bisegmentectomy IV-V. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VII (3.9 cm). No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Single 3.9 cm metastasis confined to segment VII, no extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
- Prior liver surgery (bisegmentectomy IV‑V) has already removed segments IV‑V; the remaining right posterior sector (including VII) can be resected while preserving sufficient parenchyma.  
- MDT comment “late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable” indicates that, in the multidisciplinary view, the lesion is amenable to curative resection without need for down‑staging.  
- Although FLR volumetry is not reported, the expected future liver remnant after a segment VII resection (segments I, II, III, VI, VIII) would normally exceed the safety threshold (>30 % in a normal liver). Therefore, surgery can be planned immediately, pending routine pre‑operative liver function assessment.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Verify that the colorectal primary has already been resected; if not, schedule colon resection (or endoscopic removal) before hepatic surgery.  
- Perform pre‑operative liver function testing (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin) and volumetric CT/MRI to confirm FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if any hepatic impairment).  
- Proceed with repeat hepatic resection: an anatomical segmentectomy of VII (or a non‑anatomical wedge if intra‑operative ultrasound shows a clear margin) using intra‑operative ultrasound guidance to ensure negative margins (R0).  
- Post‑operative (adjuvant) systemic chemotherapy is recommended because of KRAS mutation and prior recurrence: 6 months of oxaliplatin‑based (FOLFOX) or irinotecan‑based (FOLFIRI) regimen, with bevacizumab if not contraindicated.  
- Enroll the patient in a structured surveillance program: CEA measurement every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the abdomen and chest at 6‑month intervals for at least 3 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio/volumetry: needed to confirm that the remaining liver will be functionally sufficient after segment VII resection.  
- Confirmation of colorectal primary status (resected vs still present) and any residual symptoms (obstruction, bleeding) that could dictate sequencing of surgery.  
- Timing of the liver metastasis (synchronous vs metachronous) and any vascular contact/invasion that might affect the technical feasibility of resection.  
- Baseline CEA level to aid postoperative surveillance and to assess tumor biology.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single metachronous liver metastasis in segment VII (3.9 cm) after a prior bisegmentectomy IV–V, without reported extrahepatic disease. The lesion is located in a posterior segment and appears anatomically accessible while preserving adequate inflow/outflow and functional reserve. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of prior limited hepatectomy, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of segment VII.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer with three liver metastases (2-4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 620 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Synchronous hepato-pulmonary involvement, discussion of sequential strategy.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has synchronous left‑sided T4N2 colon cancer, three liver metastases (2–4 cm) and bilateral pulmonary nodules. No systemic therapy has been administered, the primary tumor has not been reported as resected, and critical anatomic details (hepatic segments involved, vascular or biliary contact, future liver remnant volume, size and relationship of pulmonary nodules to vessels/bronchi) are missing. Because successful resection would require (a) control of the primary tumor, (b) down‑staging of hepatic and pulmonary disease with systemic chemotherapy, and (c) confirmation of adequate FLR and resectability of lung lesions, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated, high‑risk disease (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months.  
- If the primary colon lesion is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation) proceed to urgent oncologic resection; if asymptomatic, defer primary resection until after initial chemotherapy.  
- Perform restaging after chemotherapy: liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define segmental involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and calculate FLR; high‑resolution chest CT (or PET‑CT) to measure pulmonary nodule size, assess mediastinal/hilar nodes, and evaluate resectability.  
- Re‑evaluate CEA trend; a significant decline supports proceeding to surgery.  
- If restaging shows:  
  • Liver disease limited to ≤4 lesions, all amenable to anatomic or non‑anatomic resection with FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy) and no major vascular invasion, and  
  • Pulmonary nodules ≤5 cm each, peripheral, and resectable with adequate pulmonary reserve,  
  then plan a staged curative approach:  
    1. Resection of the primary colon tumor (laparoscopic or open, according to local factors).  
    2. After recovery (≈4–6 weeks), perform hepatic resection (potentially combined with portal vein embolization if FLR marginal).  
    3. Once hepatic recovery is adequate, proceed to pulmonary metastasectomy (video‑assisted thoracoscopic surgery or open, depending on nodule location).  
- If any site remains unresectable after chemotherapy, continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques (RFA/MWA for liver, stereotactic body radiotherapy for lung) as bridge to possible future surgery.  
- Throughout treatment, maintain multidisciplinary surveillance and discuss any new lesions at MDT meetings.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Confirmation of whether the primary colon tumor has already been resected or requires urgent surgery.  
- Histologic grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.  
- Detailed hepatic anatomy: specific segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, arterial anatomy, and FLR ratio compatible with safe resection.  
- Liver MRI results to clarify the above hepatic details.  
- Exact size and anatomical relationship of each pulmonary nodule to bronchi and vessels, and presence of mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy.  
- Results of an FDG‑PET scan to exclude additional occult metastatic sites.  
- Information on any systemic therapy already administered.  

These missing elements are essential to move from “Potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right colon adenocarcinoma, four liver metastases (1.5-3.8 cm) and nodular peritoneal involvement at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-peritoneal disease, not curable upfront, discussion of induction chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: The presence of nodular peritoneal disease precludes an immediate curative operation. Definitive judgment requires (a) a quantified peritoneal cancer index (PCI) and assessment of peritoneal distribution, and (b) detailed hepatic anatomy (segmental location of the four lesions, vascular/biliary involvement, and future liver remnant volume). Both pieces of information are currently missing, and down‑staging systemic therapy is needed before any surgical plan can be formulated.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic induction chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or a comparable regimen) to target both hepatic and peritoneal disease.  
- After 2–3 months, repeat high‑quality contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and a dedicated CT or PET‑CT to re‑stage liver lesions, evaluate vascular relationships, and assess peritoneal burden.  
- Perform diagnostic laparoscopy with PCI scoring; if PCI is ≤10–12 and disease appears resectable, proceed to a combined curative approach:  
   • Right hemicolectomy (primary tumor resection) – either first or simultaneous depending on intra‑operative findings.  
   • Liver metastasectomy (anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing resections) ensuring an adequate FLR (≥30 % in a normal liver).  
   • Cytoreductive surgery with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) for the peritoneal nodules.  
- If PCI is high, liver disease remains extensive, or FLR is insufficient, continue systemic therapy and consider palliative measures (e.g., systemic therapy alone, best‑supportive care).  
- Throughout treatment, monitor CEA trends and reassess resectability after each systemic cycle.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Histologic grade and molecular profile of the primary tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status).  
- Confirmation of whether the primary colon lesion has already been resected and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms.  
- Precise hepatic segmental involvement, vascular/biliary contact, arterial anatomy, and FLR ratio.  
- Results of liver‑specific MRI and any prior systemic therapy received.  
- Timing of metastases (synchronous vs metachronous).  
- Detailed peritoneal disease assessment: total PCI, regional PCI, specific sites, involvement of hepatoduodenal or hilar ligaments, and FDG‑PET findings.  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 69 years old, T3N1 rectal tumor with two liver metastases and an isolated left pulmonary nodule at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 210 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, possibility of a combined approach depending on response.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
- The case involves synchronous rectal cancer (T3N1) with two liver metastases and a solitary left‑lung nodule, which MDT describes as “limited hepato‑pulmonary involvement.”  
- However, critical anatomic details required to confirm surgical feasibility are missing: size, segmental distribution, vascular or biliary involvement of the liver lesions, FLR ratio, and precise pulmonary nodule characteristics (size, relationship to bronchi/vessels).  
- The primary rectal tumor has not been reported as resected and its need for neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy is unknown.  
- Because these missing pieces directly determine whether a safe, curative‑intent operation can be performed, the lesions are considered potentially resectable pending further staging and neoadjuvant treatment.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Neoadjuvant systemic therapy: Initiate a RAS‑wild‑type–directed regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± cetuximab) for 2–3 months to assess tumor biology, achieve possible downsizing of liver metastases and the pulmonary nodule, and treat occult micrometastatic disease.  
- Neoadjuvant rectal treatment: If the rectal primary has not yet been resected, give long‑course chemoradiotherapy (45‑50 Gy with concurrent fluoropyrimidine) followed by a short interval before surgery, as per standard T3N1 protocol.  
- Restaging after systemic therapy: Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT, and obtain an FDG‑PET/CT to confirm metabolic response of the lung nodule and exclude additional occult disease.  
- Assess resectability: Review imaging for liver lesion size, segmental location, proximity to major vessels/ducts, and calculate FLR (target ≥ 30 % in a normal liver). If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization before hepatic resection.  
- Surgical plan (if restaging confirms resectability):  
  1. Stage 1 – Low anterior resection (or appropriate sphincter‑preserving surgery) of the rectal primary with total mesorectal excision, performed either before or after liver surgery depending on operative risk and multidisciplinary consensus.  
  2. Stage 2 – Parenchymal‑sparing liver metastasectomy (anatomical or non‑anatomical) of the two lesions, aiming for negative margins (R0) while preserving adequate FLR.  
  3. Stage 3 – Wedge resection or segmentectomy of the solitary left‑lung nodule, preferably in the same operative session if pulmonary function permits, otherwise as a staged thoracic procedure within 4–6 weeks of hepatic surgery.  
- Adjuvant therapy: After complete (R0) resection, resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3–6 months of oxaliplatin‑based regimen) and consider postoperative radiotherapy to the pelvis if indicated by pathological risk factors.  
- Surveillance: Serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Primary tumor status: whether the rectal lesion has already been resected or requires neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy.  
- Histologic grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.  
- Detailed liver lesion characteristics: maximum/minimum diameters, involved hepatic segments, presence of vascular or biliary contact/invasion, and arterial anatomy.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and compatibility with safe resection.  
- Liver MRI results to refine lesion mapping.  
- Pulmonary nodule specifics: size, exact lobar location, relationship to bronchi/vessels, and FDG‑PET confirmation of metastatic nature.  
- Confirmation of any prior systemic chemotherapy administered.  
These missing items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with four bilobar liver metastases. CEA 900 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. Liver MRI: segment VII lesion invading the IVC over 1 cm.
MDT Discussion: Caval invasion requiring multidisciplinary surgical evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The liver MRI shows a segment VII metastasis with >1 cm IVC invasion, which makes a curative hepatectomy technically demanding and requires vascular reconstruction. Definitive resectability cannot be confirmed until (a) complete thoraco‑abdominal staging CT (or PET‑CT) rules out extra‑hepatic disease, (b) the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio is calculated to ensure sufficient postoperative liver volume, and (c) the status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not) is known. These missing pieces of information are decisive for planning a safe liver‑IVC resection. Therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending those prerequisite assessments (and, if needed, neoadjuvant systemic therapy to downsize the IVC involvement).

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging: obtain contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or bone metastases.  
2. Assess hepatic functional reserve: calculate FLR ratio using volumetric CT; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % in compromised liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
3. Determine primary tumor status: if the left‑colon primary has not been resected, schedule a curative colectomy (either before or simultaneous with liver surgery, depending on patient fitness and extent of liver resection).  
4. Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because of high CEA, multiple bilobar lesions, and vascular invasion; aim for 2–3 months of treatment to assess tumor biology and possibly shrink the IVC‑invasive lesion.  
5. Restage after chemotherapy with repeat liver MRI and CT to evaluate response of the IVC‑invasive metastasis and to re‑measure FLR.  
6. Multidisciplinary surgical planning: if the IVC involvement remains resectable, plan a right‑posterior (segment VII) hepatectomy with en‑bloc IVC segmental resection and reconstruction (using a prosthetic graft or autologous patch), ensuring vascular control and adequate hepatic inflow/outflow.  
7. If FLR is inadequate after planned resection, perform PVE before definitive liver surgery or adopt a two‑stage approach with interval hypertrophy.  
8. Post‑operative management: resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy as adjuvant therapy; consider targeted agents (anti‑EGFR) given RAS‑wild type if disease persists.  
9. Follow‑up: serial CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (affects prognosis).  
- Confirmation whether the primary left‑colon tumor has already been resected.  
- Thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) and abdomen‑CT results to exclude extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Exact size of each liver lesion (maximum and minimum diameters).  
- Detailed arterial anatomy and relationship of lesions to hepatic inflow/outflow structures.  
- Assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetry.  
- Status of systemic therapy already given (if any) and timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous).  
These items are most critical to finalize resectability and to design the optimal surgical‑oncologic sequence.

Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases, including a segment VII lesion invading the IVC over ~1 cm, without reported extrahepatic disease. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only in a highly selected setting, after tumor downsizing and multidisciplinary vascular assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships and a chest CT scan.
• Given the high CEA level (900 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate FOLFOXIRI combined with anti-EGFR therapy given RAS wild-type status as discussed in MDT.
• BRAF wild-type does not modify the surgical indication.
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
